query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Enriching near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles with a higher proportion of an element having a lower atomic diffusion activation barrier (e.g., Mo) creates a compositional gradient that promotes local segregation and secondary phase formation at elevated temperatures, thereby reducing structural and chemical stability compared to uniformly mixed nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled compositional gradient by increasing the fraction of a low-diffusion barrier element during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Thermal treatment or operational exposure within catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Local elemental segregation and formation of secondary phases at specific compositional regions.
generation.mechanism: The locally enriched low-diffusion barrier element diffuses faster under high-temperature conditions, which promotes atomic rearrangements and drives segregation. This segregation undermines the benefits of high configurational entropy that typically stabilizes the uniform alloy structure, leading to phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline equiatomic nanoparticles, those with a controlled compositional gradient will show increased evidence of elemental segregation and possibly secondary phase formation when subjected to thermal operating conditions.
generation.baseline: Uniformly mixed, near-equiatomic nanoparticles without a compositional gradient.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected when the enrichment exceeds a threshold level where the increased local concentration significantly lowers the effective diffusion barrier, with the outcome dependent on both the degree of compositional deviation and the specific thermal exposure parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of enrichment and the onset as well as the extent of segregation remains uncertain, and variations in processing conditions or other elemental interactions may modulate this behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: one set with a uniform near-equiatomic composition (baseline) and another set with a controlled compositional gradient that enriches the low-diffusion barrier element. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing protocols within the catalytic/thermoelectric range (e.g., 773–1173 K) for extended durations.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (and/or synchrotron diffraction) for phase identification and lattice constant measurements
Transmission electron microscopy for detecting microstructural inhomogeneities and secondary phase formation
Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to assess compositional uniformity vs. segregation
Diffusion coefficient assessments via appropriate kinetic measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles with the compositional gradient do not display increased elemental segregation or secondary phase formation relative to the equiatomic baseline under the same thermal conditions, then the hypothesis that the controlled gradient promotes instability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The drive for this segregation reaction to proceed was found to be negligible (close to 0 eV) or unfavourable for all stoichiometries apart from those that contained the highest and lowest concentration of Mo (51.9 at.% and 3.7 at.%, see figure 8). The lower and more favourable segregation energies at the extremes of the compositions considered in figure 8 imply that they are not stable. Configurational entropy can be considered to understand how temperature may affect the drive for Mo segregation. The compositions at the extremes of the Mo content considered remain unstable to temperatures exceeding 2000 K. The other compositions were found to have positive segregation energies (unstable) above 900 K, indicating that the epsilon phase containing approximately 10–40 at.% of Mo is stable. The instability of the phases that contain 3.7 at.% and 51.9 at.% Mo is in agreement with the experimental observations of the system, which predict the formation of the σ-phase (high Mo concentrations) or FCC phase (low Mo concentrations). Further work that considers the secondary phases should be carried out to refine the prediction of the maximum and minimum Mo concentration in the epsilon phase

The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D).
